narrative.text: Fig. 1.1.1, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. Seven colour-coded phases — 01 assessing the current state and enabling environment; 02 establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; 03 defining the future state; 04 planning the enterprise architecture; 05 determining health content requirements; 06 M&E of digital health implementations and fostering data use; 07 implementing, maintaining and scaling — each with its steps. Resource tiles are placed against the phases they serve and marked PDF or online. They include the WHO Digital Health Atlas, the WHO/ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, the ITU SDG Digital Investment Framework, TOGAF, Open HIE, the WHO SMART Guidelines, the WHO MAPS toolkit and the ADB Total Cost of Ownership Tool. The 'Digital implementation investment guide (this document)' tile is highlighted spanning phases 02 to 05. This chart is the original of the versions reused in later WHO handbooks.

between: The development of a digital health enterprise is a
dynamic process (Fig. 1.1.4). Depending on your country’s
context, needs and constraints, you may reorder the
steps taken during each phase or even the overall
process. Or you may need to revisit earlier phases as
your national digital health ecosystem and health needs
change over time, requiring new strategic plans and
different digital health interventions. Within a broader
ecosystem of valuable documents, tools and processes
important to planning and implementing digital
health, this document focuses on several important
phases, providing specific steps and outputs, which are
harmonized with the concepts, frameworks and terms of
these other prominent digital health resources.
Essential processes of national digital health implementations.

narrative.text: Fig. 1.1.4, 'Essential processes of national digital health implementations'. A left-to-right flow runs DIGITAL HEALTH STRATEGY → INVESTMENT ROADMAP → ENTERPRISE ARCHITECTURE → APPLICATION WITH INTERVENTIONS → SCALE, INSTITUTIONALIZE AND SUSTAIN, with a feedback arrow from scaling back to applications. Inputs feed in from above: national health priorities (into the strategy), the national inventory of digital assets (exchanged with the roadmap and architecture) and health-programme-specific needs. Governance mechanisms and a data use culture support from below, and the digital maturity of the country informs the strategy. A shaded region labelled DIIG encloses the architecture, applications and scaling steps — the part this guide covers. At the bottom sit the national eHealth strategy building blocks: leadership and governance; strategy and investment; legislation, policy and compliance; workforce; infrastructure; standards and interoperability; and services and applications.

narrative.text: Fig. 3.1, 'Adaptation of CRDM approach for defining health system challenges' and requirements. Three columns. BUSINESS PROCESS ANALYSIS, 'Think — how do we do our work now?': define goals and objectives, determine the health programme processes to target, map the user journey and workflow, and identify pain points. BUSINESS PROCESS REDESIGN, 'Rethink — how should we do our work now?': examine tasks and workflow, identify inefficiencies, restructure them, and select digital health interventions for the prioritized health system challenges. REQUIREMENTS DEFINITION, 'Describe — how can an information system support our work?': define the tasks for the optimized processes, describe how business rules are implemented, check that the enabling environment can support the interventions, define what the interventions should do from end-user needs, and determine whether existing ICT systems can be leveraged.

between: Health programme processes, also called business
processes, consist of a set of activities or tasks
performed together to achieve the objectives of the
health programme area or health system (51). Processes
involve different personas and may cross multiple levels
of the health system. For example, within the area of
antenatal care, health programme processes can include
activities associated with identifying pregnant women,
generating demand for services, monitoring supplies and
commodities, managing and following up with clients,
and reporting (see Fig. 3.1.1.1).
Start by identifying all of the priority processes for your
health programme. For each of the identified processes,
list the objectives, the inputs needed, the expected
outputs, the specific sets of tasks that make up the
process and the expected outcomes. Describe tasks in
as much detail as possible, and include every step of the
process.
The process matrix in Fig. 3.1.1.1 illustrates health
programme processes for an immunization information
system. In this example, the Expanded Programme on
Immunization (EPI) constitutes the health programme,
with the goal of providing universal immunization for
all children (52). Within the EPI health programme,
there may be a variety of processes, such as stock
management and patient management for tracking
vaccination history. These processes have a set of tasks
that one of the personas needs to carry out, such as
registering clients, ordering stock and recording stock
levels. See Annex 3.1 for a process matrix worksheet.
Process matrix illustrating three example processes within a typical
vaccination programme.

narrative.text: Fig. 3.1.1.1, 'Process matrix illustrating three example processes within a typical vaccination programme'. A table with the columns Process, Objective, Task set and Outcomes, holding four rows. A Patient management keeps a database of all newborns and their vaccination history (register, search, maintain), leading to more complete registration. B Vaccination management ensures every infant receives all scheduled doses (define the schedule, plan, send reminders, register vaccinations, monitor coverage), leading to more timely vaccination and higher coverage. C Stock management keeps vaccines available while minimizing wastage (order, receive, store, count, monitor balances and expiry), leading to higher availability and lower wastage. D Service delivery ensures quality vaccination services (counsel, diagnose, dispense, refer, update the record, schedule the next visit), leading to correct protocol, timelier vaccinations and better documentation.

narrative.text: Fig. 4.2.1, 'Roles and contributions of component “building blocks”' to a national eHealth environment. Two groups of building blocks, each block paired with its contributions. ENABLING ENVIRONMENT: leadership, governance and multisector engagement (direct and coordinate eHealth nationally, align with health goals, support change); strategy and investment (a responsive national strategy and plan, with financing aligned to priorities); legislation, policy and compliance (national policies and a legal and enforcement environment that builds trust); workforce (eHealth knowledge and skills, networks, and education and training programmes); and standards and interoperability (consistent, accurate collection and exchange of health information). ICT ENVIRONMENT: infrastructure (networks, core services and applications for information exchange across boundaries) and services and applications (the means of delivering health content and managing information, for the public, patients, providers and others).

narrative.text: Fig. 4.5.1, 'Considerations for designing a digital health enterprise'. A checklist of five ticked considerations, each with guiding questions. Identified pain points and health system challenges: what challenges did the stakeholders identify, and are digital interventions appropriate or should non-digital approaches also be considered? Evidence base and experience with the digital health intervention(s): has it been shown to address the challenges, will more than one be needed, and has it been tested at the necessary scale? Enabling environment: can the enabling and ICT environment support it, and what precautions are needed (see Chapter 5)? Requirements: how well does the enterprise meet user needs and stakeholder expectations, and does it fit the existing culture, language and workflows? Linkages to other ICT enterprises: are other interventions being implemented in the context, and can they be leveraged?

mHero – using data standards to effectively integrate
mHero combines three technologies – IntraHealth’s iHRIS software, UNICEF’s RapidPro and Jembi’s OpenHIM
– into a powerful communication tool for ministry and health workers (90).
iHRIS is open source health workforce information system software used to capture and maintain
information for planning, managing, regulating and training the health workforce. RapidPro is an open source
platform for building an interactive messaging system. OpenHIM is an interoperability layer for standards-
compliant health information exchange, such as OpenHIE.
The combined tool, mHero, allows the MOH to instantly send information to health workers’ mobile phones
and enables health workers to send time-sensitive information back to ministry officials. This was done
through rigorous adoption of open international standards, such as HL7 FHIR, for health data exchange, based
on the OpenHIE framework. By using these standards, information about the health workers could be derived
from the health workforce registry (iHRIS) and then used by the RapidPro messaging system to seamlessly
communicate with health workers around the country (see Fig. 5.6.2). For example, information on the health
facility associated with the health worker could be used as a way to target the messaging to health workers.
Furthermore, the open source and open standards approach means that the mHero platform does not depend
on any specific piece of software, which allows MOHs to readily integrate mHero into their HIS.
Fig. 5.6.2. 	 How mHero integrates digital health interventions using standards.

narrative.text: Fig. 6.3.2, 'OpenHIE architectural diagram illustrating mechanisms for interoperability across different applications'. Within a DIGITAL HEALTH PLATFORM, the OpenHIE component layer holds business domain services — (1) logistics management information system, (2) shared health record and (3) health management information system — and registry services — (4) terminology services, (5) client registry, (6) facility registry, (7) health worker registry and (8) product registry. Beneath them, (9) the interoperability services layer provides authentication, an interlinking service and entity mapping. Below the platform sit (10) point-of-service applications: mobile system, electronic medical record, health management information system, lab, pharmacy and logistics management information system. A legend defines each numbered component — for example, that the interoperability layer receives all communications from external services and orchestrates data exchange with the component layer. Adapted from OpenHIE architecture v2, 2019.

narrative.text: Fig. 7.1.1, 'Phases of implementation'. Five phases run left to right in nested shaded regions: DEVELOPMENT & SETUP → DEPLOYMENT → INTEGRATION & INTEROPERABILITY → SCALE → SUSTAINED OPERATIONS. increasing the use of high-quality data to improve immunization coverage (100). It provides a clearer picture

project evaluations and reports. The following are some key findings from the review: interconnected and
comprehensive strategies provide stronger results; data use leads to increase of quality of data; and efforts to

BID Initiative: Building a culture of data use
What does a culture of data use look like on the
ground? For Oliver Mlemeta, a nurse at the Usa
River Health Facility in Tanzania, it means she will
be trained on how to use data in a meaningful way
so that she can better serve her patients. Simplified,
automatically generated reports will reduce the
chance of error and allow her more time to do
what she loves most: care for patients. A monthly
dashboard tells her how her facility is performing
compared to neighbouring health centres and allows
Oliver to adjust services accordingly. If she has
questions, she can reach out to her peers using the
WhatsApp platform, a communication forum where
health workers provide peer support as they adopt
A primary goal of the BID Initiative was to improve
data use at all levels of the health system (see
Fig. 8.3.5). Building a culture of data use requires
products that ease data collection and visibility,
policies to support the culture and people who
can enforce the policies by establishing effective
practices. To this end, BID introduced a number
of different tools and approaches to strengthen
data use, including data-use guides, readiness
supervision that complemented the use of the EIR.

labels: An important component of sustaining a digital health enterprise is sharing lessons learned with the larger
community. Here are a few from the BID Initiative that consider policy, technical, institutional and financial
Work from the beginning with a core group of stakeholders across the government and other key
organizations. This will ensure a complete understanding of the challenges to be addressed and that the
solutions address those challenges and meet end-user needs.
Build key champions within the government and key stakeholder groups. These champions are essential to
advocate for adopting solutions and long-term funding.
Balance the need for a “proof of concept” (seeing it to believe it works) with the need to begin sustainability
planning. The key issues of technical capacity, policy environment and financing need to be considered from
Create a realistic, shared vision among partners and the government from the start. This vision will cover
what needs to be in place for sustainability (infrastructure, policy, capacity and financing) and determine
how to implement process or system changes.
Secure costing data as quickly as possible (including cost estimates if necessary). This will build
understanding of both the level of financing required and the savings possible in other budget areas because
of greater efficiencies and smoother processes.
Adapted from BID Initiative briefs: recommendations and lessons learned: sustainability (108).

narrative.text: Fig. 9.2, 'Critical sustainability elements'. Four interlocking puzzle pieces, each annotated. POLICY: understand the country's policy environment, including gaps in existing policies and strategies. TECHNICAL: map government capacity to manage solutions over the long term, and develop a capacity-building plan for human skills and infrastructure. INSTITUTIONAL: identify the level of engagement and participation across the health system in the design and adaptation of solutions. FINANCIAL: ensure the cost of maintaining and replacing solutions is feasible for the government and built into the right funding mechanism. It appears inside the 'BID Initiative: Sustainability' case study, adapted from the BID Initiative briefs.
